Midterm elections typically go poorly for an incumbent president’s party. But the 2026 election delivered the kind of resounding rebuke that feels more like a reckoning. Across America, a blue wave has crested deep into red territory, washing through many of President Trump’s formerly safe spaces, endangering his preferred candidates and putting his presidency—and his broader MAGA coalition—at risk of a historic collapse.

If this is America’s response to what has been almost two years of a president flouting norms, driving up prices, breaking promises, raking in billions of dollars, and running roughshod over ethical guardrails, it is an unmistakably emphatic one. Democrats, independents, and Republicans turned out in massive numbers to showcase their displeasure with Trump and his party, flipping the Senate and making the GOP sweat even in contests that were not previously considered competitive.

An easy win by Senator Jon Ossoff, in what was once expected to be a tough race, was an early sign of what was to come throughout Election Night. “The American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame-duck President Donald J. Trump,” the Georgia Democrat said to raucous cheers at his victory party. “The first light of dawn is on the horizon.”

Ossoff’s victory itself wasn’t a particular surprise for Democrats, but the fact that his watch party could celebrate to the strains of Kool & the Gang’s “Celebration” before 8 p.m. set the tone for the night. The deluge of Democratic gains quickly flooded across the South. In South Carolina, which has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, Annie Andrews prevailed over the incumbent Senator Darline Graham. Andrews’s ascendance was a sign of how quickly the political winds have shifted in Democrats’ favor just two years after Trump’s victory left the party rudderless and despondent. “It’s about the pain people are feeling, decisions that are being made in Washington, D.C., that have resulted in record high gas and diesel prices,” Andrews told my colleague Madeleine Carlisle on Election Day.

Across the border, Roy Cooper won his race handily in North Carolina—a state Trump carried in 2024. The state’s former governor had run perhaps the most boring and low-key campaign of all Democrats vying for the Senate in competitive states. Cooper’s victory appeared so assured that top Republican super PACs shifted their spending away from the contest toward defending seats in traditionally solid-red states, including  Kansas, in early October. Just shy of an hour after polls closed, Cooper posted a video on social media to thank voters: peaceful scenes from across North Carolina, with no spoken words except Nina Simone’s “Feeling Good.”

[Read: The beginning of the end for Trump]

From there it was on to more challenging targets, including the elusive dream of turning Texas blue. Supporters of the Senate nominee James Talarico gathered at a performing-arts center on the banks of the Colorado River, with sweeping views of the Austin skyline. They ate street tacos and ice cream from food trucks, and drank beers from a bar as news coverage played on a giant screen. The screens were on CNN when the race was called and cheers of “USA! USA! USA!” broke out, followed by “Tal-a-rico! Tal-a-rico! Tal-a-rico!” About a minute later, the governor’s race was called for Gina Hinojosa. The screams grew even louder. People jumped and hugged. Others had tears in their eyes. “I’m feeling great! We’re winning!” Mario Jimenez, a 54-year-old salesman who drove four hours from Laredo with his wife, said. He kept repeating exclamations. “This is great. Fantastic. Amazing. It’s a true blue wave!”

As the depth of the Democratic victories sunk in, Republicans looked for a scapegoat, with some turning their attention toward the man who has reshaped the party in his likeness over the past decade.

“It’s hard for me to think of a White House that has done more to sabotage their own fellow members than this one has,” Marc Short, former chief of staff to Vice President Pence, wrote on X as the result trickled in. The election results showed, he added in another post, that “voters don’t like” global tariffs, the government taking stakes in private companies, and price controls.

Trump tried to put his thumb on the scale in unprecedented ways for this election, asking that voters to pretend he was on the ballot, and they repudiated him. He pushed out Republican incumbents he considered insufficiently loyal and replaced them with acolytes who lost. He urged Republican states to redraw their congressional districts years before the decennial census, an attempt that appears to have backfired. He dismissed Americans’ concerns about inflation and called the skyrocketing cost of living a “hoax,” even though groceries and gas got even more expensive after he started a war. In the closing week of the election, he spoke in great detail about his efforts to redecorate the nation’s capital and an Ohio senator’s physique.  

Even so, Democrats were in shock when the results came in, seeking to make sense of how their party, so despondent just two years ago, had managed to become a force in so many parts of the country. Trump had seemed unstoppable after winning in 2024, barreling into traditionally Democratic territory and then governing with a maximalist approach to presidential power. “Chaos, corruption, a failing economy, a catastrophic war: Donald Trump is historically unpopular, and Republicans are paying for never standing up to him,” Joel Payne, the executive director of MoveOn, told me.

But a decisive victory doesn’t mean that legislating will come easily under a president who gives Congress little credence and has said that he plans to circumvent a body controlled by Democrats, labeling himself “Mr. Veto.” Speaking on Fox News on Election Night, Trump laid out his vision of how a divided government would work over the next two years. “They’ll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them,” he said, predicting that Democrats would eventually negotiate after “a couple months of vetoes.” Before any of that can happen, the party must also deal with its internecine battle between progressives and moderates, which will not be put to rest by an Election Night that saw members of both wings of the party elected.

On Tuesday, none of that mattered, at least for a night. In Phoenix, pop music blared and Dos Equis flowed at the Arizona Democratic Party’s watch party. Senator Mark Kelly told the crowd that Democratic gains reflected just how fed up Americans are “with the chaos, the corruption, the rising costs and a wanna-be-dictator in the White House.” Dora Cruz, a 69-year-old retiree who worked in customer service and wore an American-flag scarf, exuded joy as she watched the results. The outcome gave her hope that she was “getting our flag back. It’s just been so ugly with all this division, corruption.”

[Read: How the Democrats beat Trump]

In Alaska, three federal employees asked a waiter at 49th State Brewing in Anchorage whether he could change a television showing a college-football game to the election results. The women worked for an agency that had been gutted by the Trump administration. The three women, all Democrats, were feverishly refreshing their phones. He looked at their faces and turned the channel.

Now they were watching what seemed like a seismic victory. One woman noted the New Mexico governor’s race. Another mentioned the Georgia victory. “This is huge,” she said.

The Alaska results still hadn’t come in, yet. “Is it too early for us to celebrate?” one of them asked the others. It was not. The Senate was called for the Democrats soon after.

Marie-Rose Sheinerman, Yvonne Wingett Sanchez, Madeleine Carlisle, Kevin Sieff, and Elaine Godfrey contributed to this report.

entry.title: The Blue Wave Is Real
entry.summary: America’s response to Trump was an unmistakably emphatic one.

entry.content:
The last time South Carolina elected a Democrat to the Senate was in 1998, and until around 8 o’clock tonight, there wasn’t a lot of reason to think that streak would end any time soon. The Palmetto State has been steadfastly Republican, launching the careers of some of the biggest stars in GOP politics, including the late Senator Lindsey Graham. With Graham’s sister running to succeed him, a continuation of Republican dominance seemed all but assured.

But tonight, South Carolina, where Donald Trump won by almost 18 points two years ago, sent a Democrat to the Senate. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, flipped a seat held by the Republican Darline Graham, who took office after her brother died in July. “I don’t imagine you’ll find anybody in South Carolina who will say, Oh, I knew this was going to happen,” said Kaye Koonce, a member at-large for the Democratic National Committee.

So what did happen? Andrews benefited from a convergence of factors that seemed impossible just a few months ago, including a Republican candidate who struggled with the realities of electoral politics, a historically favorable environment for Democrats, and downballot organizing that helped turn out voters across the state. “The stars aligned,” Jaime Harrison told me. (The former chair of the DNC ran to unseat Lindsey Graham in 2020 and lost by more than 10 percentage points.) “We had a superior candidate. Darline Graham may be a very nice woman, but she wasn’t ready to be in the United States Senate.”

[Read: Repudiation]

A majority of South Carolinians appeared to agree. Darline Graham was a surprise pick when Trump tapped her to fill out her brother’s term soon after his death. Graham then stunned many by announcing she wanted to run to serve a full term. A political novice, she struggled on the trail and made early gaffes that haunted her, including saying “national security is not my thing” in a primary debate against her opponent, Representative Ralph Norman. At times, it seemed almost as if Graham didn’t really want the seat. She hardly campaigned and she didn’t raise a lot of money. (Graham pulled in less than $600,000 during the first two weeks of October, while Andrews raised $4.5 million.)

After polls showed a tightening race, Trump stumped in the state twice last month to try to save Graham. But it wasn’t enough—and, in some areas, his presence may have even hurt her. ( Civiqs’s state-by-state tracker found that as of today, his approval in South Carolina was down to just 40 percent.) Neither did it help that some Republicans had launched a grassroots write-in campaign for Norman after his defeat, and that his son, Warren Norman, wrote an op-ed titled “Why This Lifelong Conservative Won’t Vote for Darline Graham,” slamming the Republican for campaigning on fear and praising Annie Andrews.

Then you had Andrews, who was able to portray herself as a Washington outsider. “I really think the story is that people, no matter if they’re traditionally voting for Republicans, Democrats, or if they consider themselves independents, they’re tired of the Washington party politics,” Andrews told me when we talked by phone on the morning of Election Day.

Andrews said she never wanted to go into politics. She’s worked as a pediatric hospitalist at the Medical University of South Carolina Children’s Hospital for 14 years, but said she became so frustrated by how policy decisions were affecting her patients that she decided to try to change careers. “I knew that those families needed a voice and that’s why I got involved. And I think that’s why my campaign is resonating and really kind of breaking through typical partisan voting patterns down here,” Andrews told me. After the Parkland school shooting in 2018, she joined the gun-control advocacy group Moms Demand Action, and in 2022 ran against Republican Representative Nancy Mace—and lost by nearly 14 points. But much has changed in the past four years.

Democratic organizing capacity has surged throughout the state—driven in part by South Carolina becoming the first state in what will be a highly competitive Democratic presidential primary in 2028. An array of Democratic hopefuls has visited the state this cycle—Gavin Newsom, Andy Beshear, Cory Booker—bringing energy and name recognition. For the first time in decades, all 124 South Carolina State House races had Democratic challengers, regardless of how safe the Republican incumbents may have been. Each one of those candidates worked to turn out the vote in their district, doing Democratic organizing that also helped Andrews. “Our theory of the case was, if you run a Democrat in every race, you’re giving everybody a choice. And when you’re giving people a choice, they turn out,” Harrison told me.

[Read: How the Democrats beat Trump]

They did turn out, with a record percentage of voters casting ballots in a midterm. Andrews won rural and suburban counties outside of Charleston that Lindsey Graham handily won six years ago. She even won rural Chester County, which Trump carried in 2024 by 17 points. Richie Gergel, a lawyer in Charleston who runs a Democratic voter-engagement group, told me that Andrews has a talent for turning out people who are “Democrat-ish”—as well as for converting Republicans. Gergel said he had been canvassing throughout Charleston and met many lifelong Republicans who said they were going to have to hold their nose and vote for the Democrat this cycle.

Of course, Andrews was also buoyed by the blue wave that swept the country Tuesday night, campaigning on the same issues that helped Democrats flip other tough seats: affordability, diesel prices, and tariffs. South Carolina has a large agricultural community that has been hammered on all three fronts. Andrews also heavily focused on the issue of health care, speaking from her experience as a doctor, criticizing the closure of rural hospitals and the surge in health-insurance premiums. Darline Graham, on the other side, ran a race that heavily focused on culture-war issues—which may resonate with the base but didn’t help with less ideological voters just looking for help gassing up their cars.

As the scale of GOP losses became apparent tonight, Trump posted on Truth Social that had he been on the ballot, “we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” We’ll never know if that was true. But his decision to back Darline Graham, an unexpected candidate whose heart didn’t seem to be in it, created an opening in South Carolina politics that many Democrats thought they would never see in their lifetime.
entry.title: The Unlikeliest Democratic Win of All
entry.summary: Few thought South Carolina was really in play until it had already flipped.

entry.content:
Campaigns are billion-dollar contests to define the choice facing voters, but no election season this century has closed quite like this. President Trump approached his task with sarcasm and shiny objects, asking voters desperate for financial help to think only of him. If Republicans did not vote, they would “go to hell,” he said with a smile. If Republicans won the House and Senate, they would get a $5,000 check that even some of his allies dismissed as fiscal absurdity. Then he told them stories, endless stories, for hours at a time—about rounded butts, strong hands, “Dumocrats,” transgender swim meets, the Vietnam War, and the blue paint he had reapplied to the Reflecting Pool. “At this point, they are not even trying,” one Republican consultant told us about the White House in the final days of the campaign. Trump would do it his way, just as the Frank Sinatra song on the president’s iPad playlist advises.

Hakeem Jeffries, the next House speaker, answered Trump’s Borscht Belt tour with relentless repetition. He declared on Fox News last month that “costs are way too high” just hours before Trump interrupted a campaign rally to ogle what he’s called the “pile of muscle” on the rump of Ohio’s junior senator. Days later, Jeffries pledged yet again that Democrats would “relentlessly focus” on affordability while Trump boasted about the nation “making a fortune” from rising gas prices. After the president joked about the high cost of a hamburger at Mar-a-Lago, Jeffries listed his priorities as “housing, health care, and the cost of gas and groceries and goods.”

The New York congressman delivered the same message nearly every day—precise paragraphs punctuated with syncopated gesticulation and excessive alliteration. Rarely had two men atop the political pyramid been more opposite. In place of Trump’s billionaire power suits and cascading bouffant, Jeffries dressed in the capsule wardrobe of middle management, his white-soled dress sneakers unscuffed, his hair always trimmed a millimeter or two shy of a clean shave. By the final days of the campaign, the Democratic leader could barely contain his delight. “They’re talking about ballrooms and body parts,” Jeffries told a roundtable of Black pastors outside Richmond, Virginia, last week while campaigning in a district that Trump won by five points two years ago. “It’s more of the same—extremism, foolishness, and corruption—or it’s dramatic change.”

Tonight Democrats won control of the House and the Senate—and vindicated the discipline of Jeffries and his fellow Democrats. But they didn’t pull it off alone. They received extraordinary help from Trump, whose tariffs and protracted conflict with Iran juiced inflation, and whose obsession with building and profit-taking rattled voters. In two short years, Democrats have reclaimed the economic issues they lost on in 2024, and Trump has squandered the confidence of his winning majority. For the first time since 2014, public polling shows that Democrats are more trusted on the economy than Republicans. This story, about how that transformation unfolded, is based on interviews with 15 people involved in the inner workings of the campaigns on either side of the aisle. At its most basic, Democrats did what they needed by maintaining a tight focus, something Trump either believed was not necessary—or was not capable of achieving.

“We had to remain committed to keeping the main thing the main thing,” Jeffries told us a few days before Election Day, during some downtime between campaign stops. “If we were going to reverse our political fortunes we had to convince the American people that we were determined to make their life more affordable.”

Two months earlier, Jeffries gathered Democratic lawmakers in the Capitol for a slide-deck presentation that quantified how their focus was paying off. He showed them April polling data from Blue Rose Research, a Democratic firm, that ranked cost of living, the economy, inflation, and health care as the first, second, third, and sixth top voter concerns. Then he showed them the problem: Voters credited Democrats with making health care the top issue but listed nine priorities they believed Democrats placed ahead of the economy, and 14 priorities before inflation.

Jeffries clicked to the next slide, an August poll result on the same questions demonstrating that Democrats had found the solution: an almost perfect alignment between voter and party priorities. Cost of living, the economy, inflation, and health care now ranked as the top four issues, in order. Voters had come to believe that Democrats were focused most on the cost of living, followed by health care as No. 2, the economy as No. 3, and inflation coming in at No. 5.

Senate strategists were seeing the same data and arguing for the same approach, especially as winning the chamber became more of a possibility. “There was a very simple solution to say, Guys, there’s an out-of-control affordability crisis that Democrats kind of missed the boat on, for whatever reason, to varying degrees in 2024, so we need to focus like a laser on that now,” Matt Canter, a Democratic strategist, told us. “Paying for gas persuades people.”

One of the most remarkable ads of the 2024 campaign cycle was a Trump attack on misplaced Democratic priorities. The spot focused on Vice President Harris’s support for taxpayer-funded sex-change operations in prisons, with a searing tagline: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” Two years later, Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic consultant, noticed how the dynamic had inverted. Trump was defending unpopular data-center construction and Flock surveillance cameras. His final televised address before Election Day was on the National Mall, not in a key battleground state, and focused on the Triumphal Arch and the new golf course he planned along the Potomac River.

“Republicans are focused on he/him,” Ferguson told us, “and Democrats are focused on you.”

The Democrats’ journey to reclaiming majorities in the House and Senate began as soon as Trump arrived back in Washington, D.C. Two weeks after Trump’s second inauguration, Jeffries described the Democratic problem as one of connection. “Maya Angelou said it best: People won’t remember what you say. They may not even remember what you do. But they will always remember how you make them feel,” he said on the comedian Jon Stewart’s podcast. “And I think what we have to do a better job of is making the American people feel that we understand the pain that they’ve been in economically for a long period of time.”

In Jeffries’ telling, economic anxiety was the leading political issue for the past four decades. Seeking relief, voters had ping-ponged between ideologies and parties—electing George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Trump, Joe Biden, and then Trump again. “What’s consistent? The American people have a constant desire for change,” he said. “Why? Because no one has solved the fundamental problem.”

[Read: The states where Democrats have the most to gain]

By that point, House Majority PAC, the independent group affiliated with Jeffries, had already done a deep dive into the 2024 results, asking for an analysis of every public remark and paid communication in each contested congressional race. The clear result: The more a candidate talked about the economy, the better they performed. What mattered most was the frequency of talking about voters’ top concern. When Democratic pollsters asked voters to pick between a binary of economic concerns and any other issue—such as crime, immigration, abortion, foreign policy, regulation—the economic concerns were chosen by 75 to 95 percent of voters. “We lost because Democrats were perceived to be out of alignment” in 2024, Mike Smith, the president of the House Majority PAC, told us.

Within weeks of the podcast taping, Jeffries and his top advisers received more sobering news: Democrats were being overwhelmed by the shock and awe of Trump’s second term—the pardoning of the January 6 rioters, the mass firing of civil servants, the closure of whole government agencies, the immigration raids, the obsequiousness of corporate leaders, the remaking of the global order. A Democratic consultant arrived with voter research that showed the average American paid attention to politics for about four minutes a week, and three minutes and 30 seconds were focused on what Trump was doing. At best, Democrats were competing for 30 seconds every seven days—about .007 percent of an average voter’s waking hours.

Jeffries concluded that Democrats could not compete on Trump’s terms. The president’s megaphone would blare louder. “We always understood simplicity and repetition is the only way to break through,” Jeffries told us about the challenge presented by Trump. “It quickly became apparent to me that the downside of his strategy, as long as we didn’t fall for it, was that the American people would conclude, Well, I may not be following all of the craziness that’s being unleashed on us, but I do know he ain’t focused on the thing that he promised he would focus on, which is to lower our costs.”

The wisdom of this plan was not always obvious to Jeffries’ caucus. The dramatic cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency led some lawmakers to demand a defense of government institutions. The abuses of immigration enforcement created constant outrage. The attacks on media outlets and university independence rattled constitutional scholars. But Jeffries demanded that the caucus find a script and stick to it. When Trump pushed through his summer tax bill last year, Jeffries urged the caucus to focus on the Medicaid cuts it would force—a proxy for the help that working people needed—even though some Democrats argued that such a message could be attacked as a defense of poverty entitlements. By the late summer, with Obamacare subsidies set to expire at the end of the year, Democratic leaders settled on a strategy of forcing a government shutdown. The question was why.

Ezra Klein, the New York Times columnist closely read by the Democratic rank and file in Congress, urged Democrats to make the shutdown about a broad range of things that were no longer normal—not just rising costs but also Trump’s corruption and authoritarian impulses. At a Democratic caucus meeting days later, Jeffries faced a divided party, including those sympathetic to Klein’s argument that the party needed to go big. But the leader pushed back, saying it should focus on only one issue: health-care costs. “It’s the right fight, and it’s a good fight,” he told his members, before quoting the late Vernon Johns, a mentor to Martin Luther King Jr.: “If you see a good fight, get in it.”

Klein told us that he came to admire Jeffries’s judgement, even if it contradicted his advice at the time. “He chose his shutdown, and he won his shutdown, and that is pretty rare for the minority party,” Klein said. “I think the Democrats have done a good job listening broadly to the public rather than narrowly to people who just vote for Democrats.”

Several Democrats told us that they also credit Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, as well as the party at large, for staying unified, both during the shutdown and throughout the remainder of the election cycle. A Democratic pollster told us that the Democratic coordination was not just a happy accident. “It was the result of a lot of advance planning, a lot of outreach to various stakeholder groups,” this person said. Lauren French, the communications director for Senate Majority PAC, the independent group affiliated with Senate Democratic leaders, told us that the major role Schumer played in candidate recruitment proved crucial; he helped persuade Mary Peltola in Alaska, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, and Sherrod Brown in Ohio to run, and he was also supportive of Josh Turek’s candidacy in Iowa and James Talarico’s candidacy in Texas. Cooper proved so strong that Democrats could pull money from North Carolina and use it elsewhere.

Trump, meanwhile, went in the opposite direction. He helped push out Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican, clearing the way for the Democratic pickup. He undercut Texas’s incumbent senator, John Cornyn, in favor of a troubled candidate, Ken Paxton, who had been impeached by his own party and faced other scandals. Republicans soon had to redirect hundreds of millions more to a state that hadn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly 40 years. Paxton then lost, as did Texas Governor Greg Abbott. After the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina this summer, Trump  selected Darline Graham, a political novice with none of her brother’s foreign-policy expertise, to replace him. Graham struggled on the campaign trail, prompting claims that she was a “nepo sister”—and yesterday, South Carolina elected a Democratic senator for the first time in more than two decades.

Since the start of his term, Trump’s approval rating has been on steady decline. But the sharpest dips in 2025 coincided with particular presidential actions: in April, weeks after Trump announced his tariff regime; in July, weeks after Trump passed his tax bill; in November, around the end of the government shutdown and a House vote on releasing the investigative files of the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Epstein scandal, Democrats realized over time, was unexpectedly tied to economic insecurity. It fed into a broader concern that elites were operating by a different set of rules. Trump’s ballroom and allegations of improper stock trading by Republicans in Congress fit within that narrative. At the House Majority PAC, strategists realized that they could turn corruption into a cost–of-living argument—things are expensive, they began telling their ad makers, because the system is rigged. “Corruption is not an abstract thing,” one Jeffries adviser told us, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private strategy. “It is not about systems and not about institutions. It is about you and your life.”

[Read: The Republicans are bolting from Trump]

Democrats already felt they were on the right path, but then, at the end of February, Trump launched a war against Iran that spiked gas prices and again pushed inflation higher. Jeffries pushed for an immediate vote to put Democrats on record in opposition, and Republicans on record in support. Then he began the argument that this, too, would be a fight about pocketbook issues, not abstract debates about geopolitics, collateral damage by the U.S. military, a war for oil, or whether Trump was usurping the Constitution by not requesting a formal declaration of war from Congress.

As the war dragged on, Republican hopes collapsed. The clearest correlation in politics in 2026 was between gas prices at the pump and the generic ballot advantage of Democrats. “All of the polling couldn’t be more clear,” a Republican consultant told us. “We were on track towards a normal midterm map prior to the war, and you can see the favorability numbers for the administration, for Republicans at large, take a nosedive after the war began.”

Another Democratic polling operation this year asked a broader question: Regardless of what you want from the election results, would you rather things stay the same as they are now or change? Eighty-five percent of voters chose change, and only 6 percent went with the status quo. The potential was enormous. “People are willing to accept change over their party controlling Congress,” Jon Fromowitz, a co-founder of the Democratic group Future Forward, told us. “People were upset enough about the way things were going that they were very open-minded.”

The only time that Jeffries and Trump formally met in person was a trap. Jeffries and Schumer were invited to the Oval Office last September, and Jeffries walked in concerned that television cameras would be there to film a staged confrontation that could rival Trump’s showdown months earlier with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

As it happened, Trump had something else in mind. He started by offering the Democrats Diet Cokes. When they declined, the sodas were delivered anyway and placed on the Resolute Desk. Then an adviser came in and put red Trump 2028 hats next to the drinks. As they debated the terms of the coming shutdown battle with House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a photographer started circling them to get shots of Jeffries with the hats in the frame. “It was the strangest thing ever,” Jeffries said afterward, trying to explain the experience to CNN. After Jeffries left for a press conference with Schumer outside the West Wing, Trump posted a video that had added animated Mexican sombreros on their heads.

Now, more than a year later, Jeffries is poised to become the leader of the House, and the first Black lawmaker to hold the position. Democrats will be able to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses, but they will still operate under the threat of a presidential veto and a 60-vote cloture rule in the Senate that will require bipartisan cooperation. As it stands, Jeffries and Trump have almost no relationship. After Trump posted a racist video that animated Barack and Michelle Obama as monkeys, Jeffries filmed his own reaction in a video in which he said, “Fuck Donald Trump.” (Trump deleted the Obama video and blamed staff for posting it.) The president has called the man who will be house speaker “lunatic, Hakeem ‘Low IQ’ Jeffries” and called for his prosecution.

[Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next]

Jeffries has argued for months that animosity toward Trump will not interfere with Democrats’ unified focus on lowering costs. He has pointed to a bipartisan housing-affordability bill, sponsored by liberal Democrats in the House and Senate, that passed in June, with 191 Democratic votes and 166 Republican votes. A more cynical party in an election year might have denied Republicans the chance for an affordability win in the summer, but Democrats moved ahead anyway, creating what Jeffries now believes can be a model. “Our view was do the right thing, and we’ll just deal with the politics of it when we have to deal with the politics of it,” Jeffries told us. “We’re running on affordability, we’re gonna win on affordability, and we have to govern on affordability.”

Democratic success also comes with notes of caution. There is a difference between winning a referendum against the status quo and winning the confidence of the American people to chart a new path forward. Democrats have the advantage on polls of economic trust because the Republican brand has fallen so far, not because the Democratic one has risen much. “I think Trump lost it,” the Democratic pollster told us, noting that polls still show no meaningful increase in the favorability of the Democratic Party.

At the same time, even those closest to Trump in the White House are hesitant to guess how he will react in the weeks ahead. The president has no record of taking responsibility for failure, and he regularly lashes out at others when things go wrong. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he posted on social media once his defeat had become clear. The official message from the White House was defiance and a recommitment to fight. But White House advisers have begun talking, quietly for now, about the “populist” issues they could get behind in the last two years of Trump’s term that would get Democratic support. Trump’s decision to create savings accounts for all American children began in the 1990s as a Democratic idea, called “KidSave,” a version of which was supported by President Bill Clinton’s administration. Hillary Clinton, in her 2008 campaign for president, proposed a similar “Baby Bonds” account. Trump’s team has been making plans to build upon them in the coming months.

But Republicans now face the same project that Democrats faced following sharp spikes in inflation under Biden: a sprint to get back on the right side of a voting majority, with only one issue at play. It is not a problem that will be easily fixed by mean tweets and diversion. It is also not a fight that Democrats are going to cede like Trump did over the last year.

After it was clear that voters had delivered Democrats control of the House, Jeffries took the stage at a victory party in Washington. “We are going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American,” he said. “We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you beginning on day one.” Behind him was a printed backdrop with the message he had repeated hundreds of times—Fighting for an Affordable America.  Simplicity and repetition had won the day.

entry.title: How the Democrats Beat Trump
entry.summary: Hakeem Jeffries pushed Democrats to focus on affordability. Donald Trump made it all about himself.

entry.content:
Photographs by Paola Chapdelaine

For decades, Texas has been the foundation of the Republican Electoral College map, holding up the red bloc of midwestern and southern states like a pedestal. Democrats have long dreamed of winning it back, only for their hopes to be crushed in election after election. And now, suddenly, James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa have accomplished what no Democrat could for more than a generation: winning statewide elections in Texas. 

Whether or not Texas is truly a battleground state now, a few things have become clear. Republicans can no longer take Texas voters for granted. Donald Trump harmed his party’s chances by propping up a weak Senate candidate in Attorney General Ken Paxton. And even Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, couldn’t buy the result he wanted. 

Heading into election day, polls showed Talarico with a modest lead over Paxton, while the incumbent Republican governor, Greg Abbott, was favored to fend off Hinojosa. But not long after the polls closed, it became clear that both Talarico and Hinojosa would win comfortably. 

The Talarico Election Night party was jubilant, with cheers erupting every few minutes as new races were called for Democrats and updated results continued showing him with a sizable lead. James Edge, a Republican mayor pro tem from Bryan, Texas, stood eating a cookie and enjoying what he was seeing. He had endorsed Talarico just after Labor Day. “My party, the Republican Party, needed a kick in the pants,” he said. “This is uncharted waters. If it holds, it’s an earthquake like we’ve never seen.” 

[Read: Trump has pushed some Texas Republicans too far]

At Paxton’s Election Night event in Dallas, party activists groaned as Fox News updated its ballot totals and the magnitude of the loss began to sink in. The Democrats even won the race for Texas railroad commissioner—a job held by Republicans for the past 36 years—as Jon Rosenthal easily defeated Bo French, who ran a race-baiting campaign that outraged the state’s growing Indian American population. Jarrod Atkinson, a Dallas-area Republican activist, walked out of the ballroom where Paxton was scheduled to speak, looking stunned. He laid the blame squarely on Trump. “The fact that he keeps telling everyone to vote like he’s on the ballot is absolutely insane,” he said. “He has said some of the dumbest things that have ever been uttered.”

Before tonight, Texas had not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, and had not chosen a Democrat for the U.S. Senate since Lloyd Bentsen, in 1988. But the state’s shifting demographics have nurtured Democratic hopes of a comeback for years. Texas, which Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024, has grown significantly wealthier, more urban, and more racially diverse even as Republicans have dominated its politics. In fact, the shift traces in part to some of the very pro-business policies that have made Texas so appealing to large corporations. During the past three decades of GOP rule, the state has offered itself as a foil to New York and California, with cheaper housing, more job opportunities, lower taxes, and less red tape. The state’s population has grown more than 8 percent since 2020, absorbing more new residents than any other. More than 300 companies have relocated their corporate headquarters to Texas since 2015, including Tesla, Oracle, and Charles Schwab. Tech employment has been growing faster in Austin than in Silicon Valley. 

Republicans like to think of the influx as a political endorsement of GOP rule. But the newcomers are more racially diverse and more likely to be college-educated than the average Texan. Over the past decade, the percentage of adults in the state with a bachelor’s degree or higher—a group that has shifted decisively to the Democratic coalition—rose from 28 to 35 percent. Hispanics, who made up 40.9 percent of the population in 2025, are now a plurality of the state’s residents.

Demographic change alone was not enough to deliver a statewide election to Democrats. But Republicans entered this Senate race with at least two additional disadvantages. The first is broad discontent about the rising cost of living, which voters seem to have directed not just at Donald Trump but also at Texas’s ruling class. Republicans of yore had campaigned on the “Texas Miracle,” touting broad economic growth. That case became harder to make amid rising prices for groceries, gas, health care, and housing. “It felt like everything was on the upswing for a long time,” Nancy Zdunkewicz, an Austin-based Democratic pollster, told us. “The bill is now due.”

[Read: The GOP’s culture-war Hail Mary]

Mike Madrid, a political consultant who studies Hispanic-voting trends, told us that the percentage of early votes in the state included more ballots cast by Hispanic voters than any other group, including white voters. “That is something I have not seen in 35 years,” Madrid said. “If the economy were doing really well right now, we would not be seeing this.” In 2024, Hispanic Texans swung heavily toward Trump. This year, they appear to have shifted right back. Madrid argues that Hispanic voters are an emerging swing demographic, more populist than ideological, and that this year they’re mad about inflation. The lesson for Democrats, he said, is that the party needs a pro-growth message and a “new southern strategy” tailored to working-class Hispanic voters across the Sun Belt states, with Texas at the center.

In the Senate race, Republicans compounded their disadvantages by nominating a deeply flawed candidate, while Democrats nominated one who positioned himself as the morally upstanding alternative. Paxton, whom Trump endorsed in the primary over the incumbent, John Cornyn, was known for a list of legal, ethical, and personal scandals far too extensive to summarize here. Dan Jackson, a truck driver and three-time Trump voter in Plano, said he “had some trouble” sorting out all the negative ads he’d seen this year. Ultimately, he voted for Abbott for governor—a safe choice, he reasoned—but went for Talarico for Senate because he doesn’t trust Paxton. 

“You’ve got, in Paxton, the worst statewide candidate to top the Republican ticket in the entire history of Republican hegemony in the state,” James Henson, the director of the Texas Politics Project at UT Austin, told us. “And then an unusually skilled Democratic candidate in Talarico, who came along at the right moment and has been able to execute better than any Democrat before him.”

When Gina Hinojosa was considering whether to run for governor, she met with Beto O’Rourke, whose campaigns for Senate and governor had electrified a hopeful Democratic base only to end in disappointment on Election Day. Someone needed to run against Abbott, the entrenched and powerful incumbent, Hinojosa told him. Should she do it? One comment stood out: “Not one person can win Texas,” he told her, according to someone familiar with their conversation. “It has to be two.” O’Rourke told her that both times he was running statewide, he felt that his campaign would have benefited from a stronger ticket.

The dynamic that emerged in 2026 was one in which Hinojosa and Talarico could work in tandem, sharing a similar message while energizing different pockets of the state. Talarico spoke openly about his faith, and had a sunny disposition that played well in rural areas. Hinojosa, a Latina woman, targeted the conservative suburban women known as MAGA moms who shared her concern about privatizing public schools. 

Talarico, in particular, ran as that rare political breed: a Democrat who seems genuinely comfortable talking about his Christian faith. He was willing to mix it up with Joe Rogan and Fox News hosts. He was careful not to mention Trump, lest he alienate the many Texans who had voted for the president but whose votes he would need.

Talarico’s final rally, held in an outdoor amphitheater filled with nearly 2,000 people, was an anxiety-filled dose of optimism. “I’m a worrywart,” Pauline Bryson, an Austin resident attending the rally, said. “But a very hopeful worrywart.” Some recalled bawling when Beto O’Rourke lost in 2018; they questioned whether it was okay to be hopeful. But this time felt different—right? Right? Through a hoarse voice, Talarico asked the crowd to be the “slingshot” to help his David beat the Paxton Goliath. 

[Read: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty]

Some 225 miles away, Paxton’s campaign sputtered to a close. Paxton’s team had planned to end his campaign with a rally at the Alamo Monday evening. They canceled the event with no explanation, and Paxton’s finale took place instead at Matt’s Rancho Martinez, a Tex-Mex restaurant next to a Quality Inn on the side of the expressway north of Dallas. About 150 supporters showed up, helping themselves to free nachos and margaritas, and the NRA handed out trucker caps and stickers. Paxton had spent the final stretch traveling the state on what he called the “Come and Take It” tour, speaking at restaurants and other relatively small venues. His slogan and the cannon imagery on the side of his tour bus were meant to channel the defenders of the Alamo, and the breakaway defiance that produced the state’s independence. But it sounded like he was inviting Democrats to take the Senate seat.

Local Republican officials warmed up the crowd with warnings that the state was on the cusp of disaster. One praised Paxton for helping defeat “the Bush cartel,” a reference to the state’s pre-Trump Republican establishment. A lot of the red-meat rhetoric was over the top, with communism, Sharia law, and forced vegetarianism looming over the taco bar. “If Texas turns blue, it’s our children and grandchildren who will be enslaved with it,” State Senator Bob Hall told the crowd. The Turkish former NBA player and political stuntman Enes Kanter, who has changed his name to Enes Kanter Freedom and more recently declared himself a woman who wants to play in the WNBA, came out to introduce Paxton. He told the audience “close your eyes and think about your daughter being in the same locker room with biological males.” There were gasps.

Frank DeSimone, a software developer and local Republican precinct official who attended the Paxton rally, told us the booming suburbs north of Dallas, where he lived, were facing “a paradox.” Rapid growth brings rapid change, he said, jeopardizing the same things that attracted so many transplants—safe neighborhoods, good schools—in the first place. It was up to Republicans to stand for a set of “Texas values” that would win suburban voters over. DeSimone said he wanted to help grow the party by defining that in a big-tent way. Did he think Texas will be an up-for-grabs purple state in ’28? “It already is,” he said.

For all his weaknesses, Paxton entered the general election with a not-so-secret weapon. Elon Musk poured almost $200 million into the state, the bulk of it to boost Paxton’s Senate bid. Musk’s home base is in the state, and he has located many of his businesses in Texas, with all the tax breaks and political connections that flow from that. On Monday morning, we paid a visit to a corner of Bastrop, Texas, that has become so identified with Musk that locals call it “Elon Land.” His tunnel-digging business, the Boring Company, is here, along with SpaceX and Starlink. Those companies have made some residents rich. But even in Elon Land, we found signs that his political reach is limited. 

Sebastyon Champion, a 38-year-old senior project manager working on the SpaceX facility, wore a Carhartt hat and a silver cross as he finished a pulled-pork sandwich at the Boring Bodega, a combination of a market, a bar, and a hair salon. He is well paid, living in an apartment complex so new that most units haven’t yet been sold, but he also noted that he paid $100 to put three-quarters of a tank into his truck that morning. He’s a conservative voter—“We have a saying here: Don’t California my Texas”—but was turned off by Paxton and his history of corruption. “Ken Paxton should be in jail,” he said. “I wouldn’t piss on him if he was on fire.” He voted for Abbott, but when it came to the Senate race, he went for a third-party candidate. In fact, over the course of several hours, in conversations with more than a dozen Texans whose livelihood depends on Musk—and in a setting directly across from a mammoth manufacturing plant the tech mogul is constructing—we could find no one who was supporting the candidate he had spent so much money to prop up.

The lingering question, which will be litigated in election cycles to come, is whether a generational political realignment is taking place in one of the nation’s largest states—or whether Democrats just got lucky this time. “People who win think it’s about them. It’s always about their opponent,” Bill Miller, a lobbyist in Austin with connections to both parties, told us. “People vote against people. That’s our culture now. If Democrats think it’s because they got all the issues, they don’t. It’s the issues that Republicans are carrying are turning people off.”

That might be true—but in two years, the GOP will still be defined by an incumbent president who is currently the most unpopular in the history of polling. Texas will be worth 40 electoral votes in the next presidential election, and there are few plausible Republican roads to victory without it. The last time a Democratic presidential candidate won the state was Jimmy Carter in 1976. Heading into 2028, Texas Democrats won’t be able to stop themselves from dreaming big. 

Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed to this report.
entry.title: How Texas Turned Blue
entry.summary: An impossible Democratic dream has finally come true.

entry.content:
The president’s party is always expected to do poorly in midterm elections, just not this poorly. The results arriving tonight are a disaster for Donald Trump—the kind of complete repudiation that the president’s opponents have spent a decade pining for, but never quite achieving. On current trends, Democrats are not just poised to claim a large majority in the House of Representatives. They are also on track to capture the Senate by winning seats they hoped for, as in Texas, and others that they had no business hoping for, as in South Carolina.

The rebuke looks too ubiquitous to be confined to the gripes of any particular subset of voters. In Miami-Dade County, in Florida, for example, the impressive Latino support that Trump built up in his 2024 win appears to have totally evaporated. Kansas is on the verge of electing a Democratic senator—for the first time in a century. Democrats in Ohio seem likely to flip both the governor’s mansion and a U.S. Senate seat. Earlier today, a (Never Trump) Republican operative in the Midwest texted me, saying, “Our party badly needs an acid lava barbed-wire enema and I’m hoping we get it tonight.” Voters heard this wish.

How did the GOP’s situation get so bad? A moralizing account might say that Trump is getting just deserts for his precedent-breaking behavior in office—the great personal enrichment, the weaponization of the justice system against his enemies, the dismantling of agencies without congressional consent. But this assumes too much about the propriety of American voters—who, after all, returned the president to office after he had tried to overturn his election loss in 2020.

The more obvious explanation for Republicans’ poor performance is economic. Having come to office by exploiting discontent with inflation under Joe Biden, Trump seemed to think that the same rules would not apply to him while in office. The president has launched trade wars against the rest of the world, increasing the costs of imported goods, in addition to passing a massive tax cut and encouraging the AI-spending boom, which have pushed up interest rates. Most disastrously, he launched a war of choice against Iran that has raised the cost of gas and diesel.

[Read: The beginning of the end for Trump]

Only 38 percent of Americans now say that they approve of the president’s job performance. Trump and his allies attempted to juice their odds of holding the House by having Republican-led states aggressively gerrymander their districts. This strategy did not work.

Unlike the president, Democrats learned the lessons of the last election: both that incumbents were vulnerable to attacks over the cost of living and that they had veered too far to the left on immigration and social-justice issues such as trans rights. The party has many sects—urban socialists, rural populists, “abundance”-pilled technocrats—that converged on a common message: the issue of “affordability,” on which Republicans were weak.

All of these factions can be expected to jockey for credit in the party’s election victory, but Democrats’ all-terrain overperformance suggests that it was Republican actions in leadership that lost the election. The president’s predilection for underwhelming candidates, including the scandal-ridden Ken Paxton as Senate nominee in Texas and the underqualified Darline Graham in South Carolina, was a factor. But most of the problem seems to have been the president’s own policy making—a drag so serious that it imperiled experienced and established Republicans such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Governor Greg Abbott of Texas.

The imminent demise of Trumpism has been predicted many times in the past decade. Even now, it cannot be guaranteed. The repudiation of Trumpism at the ballot box does not spell its demise even in the Republican Party. Such is the president’s hold among his loyal base. Democrats will be able to stymie the White House with budget battles and constant investigations, and will likely be in a position to block any Supreme Court nominees.

Tonight’s outcome does not so much foretell a powerless president as it does an angry and perhaps even more disinhibited one. All of the president’s signature policy decisions of this term—the Iran war, the trade wars, special military operations in Venezuela and the Caribbean Sea—were launched without any congressional input whatsoever. Although Congress will more jealously try to guard its power under Democratic control, the imperial presidency is well entrenched. Trump’s power will eventually end—but only after one more election.

entry.title: Why Republicans Lost So Big
entry.summary: Trump’s opponents have spent a decade pining for an outcome like this.

entry.content:
President Trump has been the dominant political figure of this century. He pulled off one of the most unlikely campaign victories in American history, and then staged the greatest political comeback. He has altered the United States’ relationship with the world, rewritten the rules and expectations of the presidency, inflamed the nation’s divisions, and changed how—and how often—Americans think about his office. He is omnipresent, and draws his power from that ubiquity.

But tonight, Trump has been forced to face his political mortality. He asked voters to make these midterm elections a referendum on him, to imagine that his name was on the ballot. They listened—and then rejected him. It is a stunning, widespread rebuke. Democrats appear poised to win the House and, if trends hold, could also capture the Senate after Americans registered their strong disapproval of the direction in which the president has taken the country over the past two years. Trump will now likely have to deal with congressional Democrats who could block his agenda and wield the power of the subpoena. He also must face the possibility that the political party he remade in his image may soon start looking beyond him. Donald J. Trump is now officially, thoroughly, a lame duck.

But we haven’t heard the last of him. He remains the commander in chief, dominates global affairs, wields the expansive power of executive orders, and remains unequaled at capturing attention. He has escaped the political graveyard more than once before, and emerged stronger. Yet for all his power, for all his volume, he cannot browbeat the unrelenting calendar: The next national election will be the one to replace him. Trump will before long begin to slip in the headlines, pushed off the front page by the presidential campaign. He’ll face the possibility of being succeeded by a Democratic president who could employ the Department of Justice to plumb the previous four years and look into Trump’s allies, friends, family, and businesses. And he’ll confront arguably his greatest fear: irrelevance.

Trump will not go quietly. It is not clear whether he and fellow Republicans will even accept the midterm results—and he has defied expectations so often that it would be a foolish exercise to set any. Tonight’s expected losses will not humble him. But they mark the beginning of the end.

Trump’s midterm campaign ended in the most ridiculous, yet predictable, way possible. For months, the president had been accused of being out of touch, of losing his once-unmatched feel for what animated his supporters. He has mocked affordability concerns while his own fortune has swelled, started a war that Americans did not want, remodeled the White House, and planned various monuments to himself. And then yesterday, he decided that the best way to push back against the accusation that he’d been consumed with vanity projects and corrupt bargains would be to deliver the final speech of the campaign cycle at the site of his most absurd, failed renovation project.

To the dismay of Republicans everywhere, Trump stood in front of the Reflecting Pool on the eve of Election Day and delivered a defense of a project that was doomed by algae and the shoddy work of a no-bid contractor. The project—which Trump had falsely claimed was derailed by vandalism—ran millions of dollars over budget and surely earned not a single vote in places such as Michigan, Kansas, and Alaska. Worst of all, the detour to revisit the Reflecting Pool distracted from Trump’s true closing message: that Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a great body.

[Read: Trump is closing from behind]

Trump was a late entrant on the campaign trail, and had to be talked into holding rallies over the past month or so. But once he was, he insisted that the election be about himself and his successes, and make no acknowledgment of any missteps or empathy for those who are struggling. He insisted that many campaign ads feature him. He demanded a first-of-its-kind midterm political convention, though few who attended the festivities in Dallas seemed happy to be there. Trump threw himself into the campaign, holding nearly-two-hour rallies night after night across the country. But these road shows weren’t quite the same as those that became the defining political event of the past decade.

They were smaller than normal, and few were outdoors (in part because of security concerns). One rally in Ohio in the campaign’s final fortnight was held in a small gym, and others featured plenty of empty seats. More striking was where the rallies were held: nearly half in deep-red states where Trump has easily won in the past and has rarely needed to campaign. That led to bigger, more enthusiastic crowds—people in a place like Corinth, Mississippi, were more excited to see Trump for the first time than, say, those in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where he has held more than half a dozen rallies over the years. But the geography also told a story: Trump had to visit Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Montana because seats in those states were suddenly in play and his faithful had to be summoned. But once there, what did Trump really have to offer?

Voters, per polling, are angry over his string of broken promises, including his vows to bring down prices, not start new wars, release the Epstein files, and deport only the “worst of the worst.” The parties of incumbent presidents traditionally fare poorly in the midterms, but Trump is also underwater on several of what used to be his strongest issues, such as the economy and immigration. He forced out multiple incumbent senators for being disloyal and backed some problematic candidates, all of which put more races into play. He gave Republican candidates very little to run on, as voters furiously reacted to an economy that seemed to benefit only the rich (a category that includes the president’s family and Cabinet). Instead, Trump tried to recycle culture-war issues from campaigns past, including fears about transgender surgeries, Muslim terrorists, and even communism.

[Read: Going hungry in Trump’s economy]

He seemed out of step not just with the public but, in many cases, with his own party. Despite warnings that AI could wipe out humanity (or at least a lot of jobs), Trump backed the nascent technology and its data centers—even as the public turned on them—because tech companies are propping up the stock market. He supported a controversial attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race that the state’s Republican governor denounced. He sided with Russia in its war with Ukraine. He threatened to once more bomb Iran. And there really was a lot of talk about butts, which will surely confuse future historians.

Americans didn’t seem to go for it. As of this writing Democrats were well on track to decisively take the House. But the story is the Senate: Democrats have already flipped North and South Carolina and easily held on to Georgia. Ohio, Texas, and other deep-red strongholds may soon join them.

As those results came in, Trump took to social media to duck blame—and contradict the central message of his campaign, writing, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Trump is now in a new place, and one he won’t like.

In his first midterm election, in 2018, Democrats gained control of the House, but that victory was offset by GOP wins in the Senate. House Democrats slowed the president’s agenda, but their 2019 impeachment effort over Ukraine only bolstered Trump’s approval ratings—and he still felt bullish about his reelection chances on the back of a strong economy. (Then, of course, came the pandemic.) Many Democrats say they’ve learned their lesson. Senior members in the party, including Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next House speaker, have been cagey as to their plans for power. The Democratic Party’s approval ratings remain low, and although not being a Republican boosted many Democrats in this year’s campaign, that won’t be the case going forward. Jeffries has signaled that he will focus on measures to try to address affordability and health-care challenges. Democrats are going to say “no” a lot, and now that it appears that they will capture the Senate too, they will likely make it difficult for Trump to confirm any of his nominees, including possible Supreme Court justices.

But the Democratic Party’s base is hungry to hold the Trump administration accountable: for DOGE’s destruction of the government, for war, for foreign business deals masquerading as diplomacy, for profiting off the presidency. Accusations of corruption against Trump and his administration have proliferated compared with in his first term. Democrats have promised to issue subpoenas and parade administration officials through the Capitol’s hearing rooms—if they agree to show up. Some close to Trump have theorized that he doesn’t mind having a foil in Washington, and that he would be comfortable tangling with congressional Democrats again. “He likes to have someone to fight—and someone to blame,” one close outside adviser told me on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal dynamics.

But Trump is leery about some of the possible investigations and does not want to be impeached again. (Democrats might be more inclined to try to oust a Cabinet member anyway.) The probes he likely faces next year could act as a preview of what would happen in 2029 if a Democratic president follows him. Trump enjoys a sort of immunity granted by the Supreme Court, and he has vowed to give preemptive pardons to many people in this administration. Yet advisers say he is unhappy at the prospect of his inner circle facing punishing investigations once he leaves office.

[Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next]

Today’s vote is a clear marker on Trump’s road to irrelevance. Many close to him believe that his driving motivation—more than power or money—is attention. And for a decade now, he has blocked out the sun, dominating the discourse in a way that no other president has in generations. But that will begin to change as Washington begins to look beyond him. Once a colossus, Trump will quickly find himself to be a secondary storyline. It’s not as if he will suddenly vanish; he’ll aim to play GOP kingmaker, and he’ll still surely inspire loyalty from his hard-core believers, even if that group shrinks. He’ll still be commander in chief, and even lame-duck presidents have broad authority when it comes to foreign policy. A return to war with Iran? A move on Cuba? Revisiting Greenland? With Trump fixated on his legacy and desperate to stay in the spotlight, anything feels possible.

Trump also may start to see the complete fealty of the Republican Party erode. This stunning midterms wipeout suggests that Trump’s instincts and influence seem to be waning, and Republicans may be more willing to defy him. As the next round of presidential contenders begins to emerge, Republicans will begin to sort out what their post-MAGA future will look like—and what role, if any, Trump plays in it.

entry.title: Repudiation
entry.summary: The president told voters to act like his name was on the ballot—and they did.

entry.content:
Long before he entered politics, Donald Trump divided humanity into winners and losers, and nothing has mattered more to him than counting himself among the former. This need drove his refusal to accept the 2020 election results—how could a man defined by winning lose?

Whatever misgivings some Republicans may have about Trump’s character or his policies, many subscribe to the theory that, if nothing else, the man knows how to win. And his aura of mastery has extended beyond his followers to the Americans who most detest him. The disgust with which many liberals regard Trump is mixed with fear and envy. His powers of persuasion are a source of endless fascination. They have launched a thousand diner safaris to explore his mystical hold on Real America, and inspired innumerable Democratic activists and intellectuals to ponder how they could create a Trump of their own.

But Trump is not a winner. He is, for the most part, a loser. In 2016, he lost the national popular vote—that is, the measure of which candidate Americans wanted to win the election—by two percentage points. His party lost control of the House in the 2018 midterms. Trump lost reelection in 2020. His sole unambiguous victory came in 2024, when he faced the clumsy fill-in candidate for an unpopular administration, against which he prevailed, almost by default.

And now he has lost again. The 2026 midterm elections are delivering a repudiation of historic magnitude to the president’s party, extending far deeper than the customary pendulum swing against the party in power. Not only did Trump’s presidency as a whole repel the electorate, but also his specific interventions in Republican primaries proved counterproductive. He handpicked Senate candidates, such as Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina, for their loyalty, assuming that any warm body could prevail in such deep-red states. Yet Graham went down to defeat, and Paxton currently trails his Democratic opponent, James Talarico.

[Read: What Donald Trump fears most]

The results help clarify the precise nature of Trump’s political talent. He does possess a certain animal cunning that allows him to home in on human weakness, among both his allies and his targets. (“Jeb’s a loser,” he said in February 2016. “The last thing we need, frankly, is another Bush.”) His speech is so ambiguous and discursive that he avoids being pinned down on particulars. These traits have made him relatively effective as a challenger, exploiting discontent with his opponents while making grand promises (a golden era of wealth, world peace) without specifying any steps he will take to achieve them. None of these skills translates to effective governing.

After his election victory two years ago, Democrats feared, and expected, that Trump would coast on the economic recovery he inherited. The post-COVID inflation that had poisoned Joe Biden’s presidency was settling back to normal, and Trump needed only to allow economic gravity to do its work while taking credit for the result.

Instead, Trump carried out the wrenching economic changes that he was unable to enact during his first term, in part because he was obstructed by his advisers and by senators from his own party. In 2017, he came one John McCain vote short of defunding the Affordable Care Act, a defeat that spared Trump’s party the political repercussions of stripping health insurance from millions of Americans. In 2025, a more compliant Republican Congress granted him his wish to gut the ACA, along with food stamps, courting the pain they had avoided eight years earlier.

After successfully taking advantage of the Biden administration’s failure to contain a surge in migrants, even winning support from millions of Latino voters, Trump proceeded to alienate swing voters with mass deportations carried out through a frequently brutal and occasionally deadly campaign of mass terror.

After promising during the 2024 campaign to bring down prices, he took active measures that economists knew would push them higher. Rather than using tariffs mostly as a bluff and settling for modestly rejiggered trade agreements for which he could claim credit, as he did during his first term, he imposed the costliest tariffs since the Herbert Hoover era.

When enterprising members of Congress decided, without Trump’s involvement, to pass a bill earlier this year to encourage more housing construction, Trump could have taken credit for their work and demonstrated at least an interest in addressing a major cost driver. Instead, angry that Republicans had failed to pass his bill restricting voting, he petulantly boycotted the signing ceremony. Declining to sign a bipartisan housing bill at a moment when housing costs are a top public concern is the political equivalent of being handed a baby and refusing to kiss it.

Most incredible of all, 10 years after he astonished the commentariat by standing on a Republican debate stage in hawkish South Carolina and declaring the Iraq War “a big, fat mistake,” Trump replicated the George W. Bush administration’s signature blunder by launching a war of choice in the Middle East without any plausible exit strategy.

Trump might have received a little bit of grace from voters if he had made visible gestures of concern for the pain that Americans felt from these policies. Presidents in the past have grasped the need to show the country that they are working hard, because, if nothing else, regular people typically assume that improving the economy is a function of presidential diligence, like a landlord fixing a leaky toilet. Instead, Trump turned his attention to decorating palaces, erecting monuments, renaming buildings after himself, and demanding awards.

He has weirdly inverted a classic populist trope, which posits that the wealth and comfort of the capital comes at the expense of the prosperity of the decent, God-fearing people of the heartland. Trump obsesses in public about his focus on the tiny area in the immediate vicinity of the White House. He devoted his closing message the day before the election to a lengthy recitation of improvements in the capital, from his war against algae to a proposed golf course, which he promised would give residents of Washington a discount. This fixation is a source of pride only for those whose chief goal for this presidency is Trump’s glorification.

The theme connecting all of these baffling choices is a misread of the 2024 election results. The MAGA cult was never large enough to win a majority of the Electoral College. Trump won because he offered an alternative to an unpopular Biden administration, and because enough of the public fondly recalled his first presidential term before COVID struck—and retroactively excused him for the consequences of his pandemic mismanagement. The myth of Trump’s political genius is primarily a by-product of this first-term good fortune. He inherited a healthy economy and had little effect on its trajectory, paradoxically benefiting from failure. The buoyant recovery created a floor beneath his approval ratings that no gaffe or scandal could crash through.

Trump, however, convinced himself that he had won because the public shared his conclusion that his first term had been a treacherous betrayal by his enemies. And so, while Trump’s 2024 coalition hinged on Americans who felt nostalgic for his first term, these same voters empowered a president determined not to repeat it.

[David Frum: Only losers play the madman]

He ruthlessly purged the bureaucracy and his party of all dissent so that he could build the dream palace of his imagination—an imperium that would silence his critics in the news media, reduce the business elite to sniveling courtiers, and venerate him as a king.

Many of these efforts have met with success. But the unwavering loyalty he has commanded within his party has come at the price of revulsion outside of it. Trump made the autocrat’s error of believing his own propaganda, thus denying himself the benefit of realistic advice that might help him avert or correct his misjudgments. And by treating disagreement as treason, he locked the exits, trapping his fellow Republicans with him as he burned down their reputation.

While the Americans who worship Trump as a culture-war champion or god-king remain enthralled, the ones who thought they were hiring him for a four-year gig to get a handle on the border and inflation regard his second term as a failure.

Those two constituencies are often conflated with each other, and Republicans have encouraged the conflation by treating his fans as the authentic Volk. In reality, Trump’s base is not synonymous with the country. His base has never constituted anything close to a national majority. Stripped of the protective gloss he enjoyed from the healthy economy during his first term, Trump has no more political magic than Jimmy Carter.
entry.title: Donald Trump Is Bad at Politics
entry.summary: The aura of mastery and domination that surrounds the president should now be permanently dispelled.

When Jon Ossoff was first elected, in January 2021, he felt a little like an accidental senator. He was 33 years old and had won by just 55,000 votes, defeating the unpopular Republican incumbent, David Perdue, in a runoff election overshadowed by President Trump’s bogus claims of voter fraud.

He doesn’t feel accidental anymore.

Ossoff cruised to reelection tonight. The final margin of victory is not yet known, but networks called the race early; soon after the polls closed, any drama was gone, even though he had been campaigning in a state that is barely purple. His triumph does not change much about the Senate’s electoral calculus overall, because Democrats were expected to hold his seat, but the decisive victory immediately propels him into the top ranks of the party and any discussions about the 2028 presidential contest.

Ossoff’s win is a testament to his deftness as both senator and candidate. In office, he has emphasized constituent services but also mastered the art of getting under the skin of Republican officials during Senate hearings, without ever seeming ruffled himself. On the stump, his campaign showed an acute sense of how to use media, even producing a new coinage—the “Ossoff angle”—to describe the upward camera perspective that his team worked to produce.

He paired these good visuals with a knack for the sound bite. In the most famous instance, in August, he slyly said that Trump “doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie.” Although he omitted her last name, the moment made the president’s assistant Natalie Harp—who was previously familiar only to political reporters and political junkies—into a prominent figure. The ensuing news cycle was both damaging and distracting to the White House. As the youngest senator, Ossoff has shown a mastery of short-form video that few of his peers can dream of.

Like many other Democrats this cycle, Ossoff benefited from the president’s unpopularity, disastrous agenda, and lack of political focus. He was running in a state that Trump had won by barely two points in 2024. Ossoff was also very lucky in his opponent. After failing to recruit a stronger candidate, Republicans landed on Mike Collins, whose many connections to white nationalists, including his son-in-law, helped sink him. But Ossoff made some of his own luck by intimidating better candidates into not running. He also showed a killer instinct on debate stages, savaging Collins over his ties to racists.

Ossoff’s campaign was impressive enough that his name is on the lips of what the columnist Russell Baker called “The Great Mentioner,” the rumor mill of possible candidates for president. During the campaign, Ossoff promised to finish his next term as senator if he were reelected. “I have zero interest in running for president,” he said during a debate. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for reelection to the Senate.” But candidates who wish to do so have squirmed their way out of stronger commitments.

What an Ossoff presidential campaign might look like is unclear. He resides more on the moderate wing of the party than on the left, but he does not have a strong ideological profile, and he has avoided confrontations with more progressive Democrats. To become a major national figure, he’ll have to define himself more clearly. And although in many ways the 2028 cycle has already begun, that election is a long way off in political time.

The skills required to run for president are also on a different tier from those needed to win at the state level, as many senators and governors have learned the hard way in the past. Ossoff’s talent outside of carefully packaged media has not yet been demonstrated on the national level. One of the backhanded compliments he gets is that someone so good at direct-to-social video messaging can’t possibly be as charismatic one-on-one. His triumph tonight guarantees that he’ll instantly be in heavy demand on television and at Democratic events across the country, where he’ll have a chance to test and hone those skills.
