This is a special Election Day edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

“The President of the United States has so singular a combination of defects for the office of a constitutional magistrate, that he could have obtained the opportunity to misrule the nation only by a visitation of Providence.” So begins one of the most withering paragraphs on politics in the history of The Atlantic. “He unites in his character the seemingly opposite qualities of demagogue and autocrat,” the passage continues, “and converts the Presidential chair into a stump or a throne, according as the impulse seizes him to cajole or to command.”

These words, written by E. P. Whipple, date back to September 1866, in the midst of a midterm election battle. The sitting president, Andrew Johnson, had been thrust into office a little more than a year earlier by John Wilkes Booth. By the time Whipple’s essay appeared, Johnson had placed himself at the center of a congressional election that would have defining consequences for the country. With the guns of the Civil War still warm, the fundamental questions of Reconstruction were at the core of national politics. The Republican majority in Congress insisted that Reconstruction must do more than simply restore Confederate states to the Union: It must secure the rights of formerly enslaved people and prevent certain former Confederate leaders from returning to political power. Johnson, a War Democrat from Tennessee who’d been nominated to balance Abraham Lincoln’s National Union ticket in 1864, took another view.

Whipple’s essays on the theatrics of Johnson’s campaign are the work of a writer at the height of his powers, but who also may be losing his mind. Whipple performed surgical eviscerations of Johnson and his allies’ efforts to nullify the Union triumph in the Civil War. Nearly blinded by his racism and opposition to Black civil rights, Johnson set himself at odds with the Republican majority, pardoning thousands of former Confederates, vetoing Reconstruction legislation, and excusing white violence on Black Americans in Memphis and New Orleans. In his essays, Whipple confronted the maddening diversions of what he called the “Johnson Party,” in which secessionists were portrayed as the true patriots, presidential overreach and usurpation were said to be in service of the Constitution, and those opposing both were seen as the real traitors. “There is no wrong anywhere,” Whipple lamented. “It is all ‘right.’”

Whipple’s shouts resonate in our own up-is-down era of politics, and in a midterm cycle in which Donald Trump, like Johnson in 1866, “sees hardly anything as it is, but almost everything as colored by his own dominant egotism.” Trump’s attempt to hold on to his party’s majority has focused on defending his record and deflecting questions about affordability and high gas prices. Some Republican candidates are distancing themselves from him ahead of Election Day, as his appearances veer into unusual tangents removed from voters’ everyday concerns (for good measure, he recently took to praising the “ass” of Senator Jon Husted of Ohio and the rapper Nicki Minaj).

Johnson, too, defined the election as a referendum not just on the nation and its future, but on his destiny in shaping it. With whispers of a possible impeachment dogging him that year, the midterms represented a showdown between the executive and legislative branches. Whipple’s essay on “The Johnson Party” came after the so-called National Union Convention, an August 1866 event that Johnson and his Cabinet had endorsed to form a new coalition that could displace the pro-Reconstruction Republican majority in Congress. In the case that Johnson’s new party failed to win, some of his supporters reportedly discussed schemes to deny Republicans power. If “Congress cannot be overcome by fair means, it will be by foul,” Whipple wrote. “In short, we are promised, on the assembling of the next Congress, a coup d’état.”

To rally support for his Reconstruction policies and preferred congressional candidates, Johnson embarked on an unsuccessful national tour. (Whipple argued that he did so “with the intention of carrying the country by assault.”) His endeavors wound up hurting, rather than helping, his cause. He took to the stump to advocate for his own interests, with Whipple noting “the immense protuberance” of the first-person pronoun throughout the president’s many speeches. Although he didn’t make the posteriors of his political allies central to his closing argument, in the end, he was deemed a “Presidential Ass” by a Michigan Republican.

Such presidential barnstorming amid a congressional election was something of a novelty that many deemed beneath the dignity of the office; the intemperate content of Johnson’s speeches made it worse. His remarks at times devolved into “a volcanic outbreak of vulgarity, conceit, bombast, scurrility, ignorance, insolence, brutality, and balderdash,” according to Whipple. When Johnson found himself assailed by hecklers (who he claimed were paid disrupters), his material took dark and strange turns. After one audience member called for the hanging of the Confederate president, Jefferson Davis, Johnson in turn suggested hanging the Republican representative Thaddeus Stevens and the abolitionist Wendell Phillips. Subsequent jeers inspired him to compare himself to Christ, betrayed by Judas and suffering on behalf of the nation at large. Governors, mayors, and other politicians were reportedly avoiding the president’s appearances, sometimes declining to welcome him or leaving town before he arrived.

As the tour concluded in the middle of September, the magnitude of Johnson’s mistake came into view. By one senator’s estimate, Johnson’s campaigning cost his preferred candidates roughly a million votes across the country—no small number in that era’s electorate. The New York Times reportedly lost nearly a third of its mostly Republican subscribers after its editor, Henry Jarvis Raymond, had openly supported Johnson and the National Union movement. Most important, the very Republicans whom Johnson had wished to displace didn’t lose seats but gained them, beyond the two-thirds majority necessary to override the presidential veto that Johnson had already used against Reconstruction legislation. And Johnson, for his part, later became the first president to ever be impeached.

The 1866 midterms took place in an entirely different world from ours. A president campaigning on behalf of congressional candidates was uncommon then, and a president routinely violating the decorum and propriety associated with the office was more uncommon yet. Whipple hoped that voters would go on to “indignantly record the most overwhelming of verdicts” against Johnson. Now, 160 years later, America once more has a president who has elevated his own ambitions above the nation’s. The people’s verdict awaits.

In the seven years I taught writing to first-year university students, I always began the semester the same way: We’d start with lessons on how to read critically. To help them, I introduced the concept of the hermeneutic circle—a fancy philosophical name for a simple idea. To comprehend the meaning of a book, readers need to analyze its individual sentences and paragraphs, but those parts can’t be interpreted without understanding how they work as a whole. In practice, this usually means reading to the end and going right back to the beginning.

The hermeneutic circle isn’t just for academics, though; it explains why some novels feel impossible to put down. You’re using it when you flip back to the opening of a mystery after you’ve reached a pivotal scene that changes what you thought you knew. Sometimes a plot twist completely flips your understanding of a character, and you can’t help but reread the novel, this time with your eyes wide open. The six books below feature unreliable narrators, jarring perspective shifts, and slow-burning reveals. As soon as they’re over, they demand to be instantly started again.

Devil House, by John Darnielle

Darnielle, the front man for the indie band the Mountain Goats, starts his third novel simply enough. Gage Chandler, a once-acclaimed true-crime writer, is sniffing out what just might be his next hit: an investigation into a 1986 unsolved double murder at a former porn shop. Some 20 years later, Chandler has moved into the scene of the crime, dubbed “Devil House,” to immerse himself in the story. But the more time he spends going through grisly source material purchased from eBay, the more he chafes at his task. Then Darnielle takes Devil House down a series of sharp left turns, and each new section feels like its own book: This meta-novel grows to include the story of the crime that inspired Chandler’s debut, The White Witch of Morro Bay, and a faux–Middle English myth rendered in Gothic font. Darnielle’s eventual return to Devil House—and Chandler’s accounting of the costs of digging up its history—is no less surprising. The reader is left to reassemble this dissection of the true-crime genre, and then to ponder what it means to arrange jumbled puzzle pieces into a coherent portrait.

[Read: 15 books you won’t regret rereading]

Dirtbag, Massachusetts, by Isaac Fitzgerald

Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional, and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing. The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13. But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life. As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive.

Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead, by Olga Tokarczuk, translated by Antonia Lloyd-Jones

Janina Duszejko, the strange older woman who narrates this Nobel Laureate’s fairy tale–tinged noir thriller, seems too caught up in her devotion to animals, astrology, and the poetry of William Blake to involve herself in anything as petty as a whodunit. But when poachers start turning up dead in Duszejko’s remote Polish hamlet in the Kłodzko Valley, she fights to make the police listen to her theory of the crimes: The animals who have long made their home in the village’s bordering forest are taking their revenge. In Tokarczuk’s hands, Duszejko is no “crazy madwoman,” as the police see her, but a prophet—the only one who can see that “animals have a very strong sense of justice.” On a second pass, with full knowledge of why Duszejko becomes so wrapped up in the murder investigations, you can better appreciate how Tokarczuk subverts the thriller’s typical form with a philosophical meditation on how humans have become all too comfortable with destroying the natural world.  

[Read: The case for rereading the high-school classics]

Loved and Missed, by Susie Boyt

I picked up Loved and Missed after seeing it recommended again and again by fellow critics as a touching, engrossing novel about the pleasures of caregiving, one that they were desperate to talk about. The book—largely narrated by a middle-aged schoolteacher named Ruth as she takes over the parenting of her granddaughter, Lily, from her drug-addicted daughter, Eleanor—is indeed poignant and charming. Ruth builds a cozy home life after deciding that Lily “was not going to have a poultice childhood, a mending service, scrappy and provisional.” Yet buzzing beneath this domestic bliss is the live wire of Eleanor’s presence and absence, and the reader is forced to wonder how Lily is affected by being the object of all of Ruth’s displaced motherly love. Then, in the last chapter, Boyt hands the reins of narration to the teenage Lily, adding a fresh charge to all that came before. No wonder we can’t stop talking about it.

She’s Under Here: A Love Story, a Horror Story, a Reckoning, by Karen Palmer

The first time I read Palmer’s memoir of fleeing her abusive ex-husband and assuming a new identity, I hardly came up for air. I was fully submerged in her recounting of 14 dangerous years of marriage—including a harrowing scene of her ex holding a gun to her pregnant belly—followed by escalating torment after she flees with her daughters. But this memoir of surviving domestic violence and then coming to terms with what it costs to start over entirely, including forged birth certificates and a fake life story, deserves to be lingered over, just as Palmer’s fear stayed with her for decades. Only on my second read, once I had made it through with Palmer to safer shores, was I able to fully appreciate the author’s persistent doubts about the choices she was forced to make, as well her haunting meditations on why she stayed for so long.

[Read: What rereading childhood books teaches adults about themselves]

Women and Children First, by Alina Grabowski

The fictional decaying coastal town of Nashquitten, Massachusetts, is a place where “it seemed like there was a death every month”—opioid overdoses, drunk driving, suicides. But the mysterious death of the aspiring artist Lucy Anderson at a high-school party stands out. Grabowski follows the ripples and rifts that led to and came after Lucy’s demise via a Rashomon-like structure, switching among the perspectives of 10 different girls and women connected to Lucy: her classmate, her guidance counselor, her best friend, her mother. Each narrator’s story offers a shard of what happened at that party, yet their points of view are contradictory and hopelessly biased, each coloring the reader’s understanding of what came before. Women and Children First is less a puzzle than a kaleidoscope, offering several misaligned but interconnected visions of the truth. The satisfaction comes not from any definitive reveal of what happened to Lucy, but from unraveling how all these characters’ actions and stories affect one another—something you can only really understand once you’ve finished the book and gone back to page one.
